claim: AMS/PCAT transporters are distributed across various phyla of both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
source: The results show that AMS/PCAT transporters are distributed across various phyla of both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence similarity network analysis shown in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claim: The largest cluster from the sequence similarity network contains members from both Gram-positive (Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, Proteobacteria) and Gram-negative bacteria (Bacteroidetes, Cyanobacteria, Spirochaetes).
source: Interestingly, the largest cluster from this SSN contains members from both Gram-positive (Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, Proteobacteria) and Gram-negative bacteria (Bacteroidetes, Cyanobacteria, Spirochaetes).
evidence: Based on sequence similarity network analysis results described in the text.

claim: The N-terminal 150 amino acids of LahT constitute an active protease domain termed LahT150.
source: Expression of the N-terminal 150 amino acids of LahT as a His6-tagged fusion protein resulted in an active protease termed LahT150 that readily removed the leader peptide from the seven tested substrates encoded in the lah cluster at the predicted double Gly motif as monitored with matrix-assisted laser desorption time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing protease activity monitored by MALDI-TOF MS.

claim: LahT150 readily removed the leader peptide from seven tested substrates encoded in the lah cluster at the predicted double Gly motif.
source: Expression of the N-terminal 150 amino acids of LahT as a His6-tagged fusion protein resulted in an active protease termed LahT150 that readily removed the leader peptide from the seven tested substrates encoded in the lah cluster at the predicted double Gly motif as monitored with matrix-assisted laser desorption time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF MS data showing cleavage products.

claim: LahT150 is highly tolerant to variation of the substrate sequence in the P' positions.
source: Given the high divergence of the core peptide sequences of these peptides (Figure 2), the enzyme is highly tolerant to variation of the substrate sequence in the P' positions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that LahT150 cleaves substrates with highly divergent core peptide sequences.

claim: ProcM-modified ProcA peptides are substrates for LahT150.
source: The ProcM-modified ProcA peptides tested (five in total) proved to be substrates for LahT150 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), producing the mature prochlorosins (Pcns) and demonstrating that the enzyme can process substrates that contain polycyclic structures in the core peptide.
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF MS data showing cleavage of modified ProcA peptides.

claim: LahT150 can process substrates that contain polycyclic structures in the core peptide.
source: The ProcM-modified ProcA peptides tested (five in total) proved to be substrates for LahT150 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), producing the mature prochlorosins (Pcns) and demonstrating that the enzyme can process substrates that contain polycyclic structures in the core peptide.
evidence: Demonstrated by successful cleavage of ProcM-modified ProcA peptides containing thioether rings.

claim: LahT150 was able to cleave the leader peptide from a group of peptides encoded in Azospirillum sp. B510.
source: Remarkably, LahT150 was able to cleave the leader peptide from a group of peptides encoded in Azospirillum sp. B510 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) even though these peptides have leader peptides of the nitrile hydratase family (for sequences see Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF MS data showing cleavage of AzoA peptides.

claim: AzoA peptides have leader peptides of the nitrile hydratase family.
source: Remarkably, LahT150 was able to cleave the leader peptide from a group of peptides encoded in Azospirillum sp. B510 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) even though these peptides have leader peptides of the nitrile hydratase family (for sequences see Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Based on sequence classification of AzoA leader peptides.

claim: N-terminally truncated ProcA2.8 peptides (with 10, 20, and 30 residues deleted) were all substrates for LahT150.
source: We first deleted the N-terminal 10, 20, and 30 residues from ProcA2.8. The resulting N-terminally truncated peptides were all substrates for LahT150 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–E).
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF MS data showing cleavage of truncated peptides.

claim: A trypsin-generated XY33a truncant containing only the C-terminal 14 residues of the leader peptide attached to the core peptide was a good substrate for LahT150.
source: We digested XY33a with trypsin resulting in a truncated leader peptide containing only its C-terminal 14 residues attached to the core peptide (for sequence see Figure 4—figure supplement 3A). This truncant was a good substrate for LahT150 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF MS data showing cleavage of the trypsin-generated truncant.

claim: A synthetic 17-amino acid peptide encoding the last 13 amino acids of the leader peptide followed by Ala-Ala-Ser-Leu was cleaved by LahT150 at the expected position.
source: Next, we purchased a synthetic substrate encoding the last 13 amino acids of the leader peptide followed by Ala-Ala-Ser-Leu. This 17-amino acid peptide was cleaved by LahT150 at the expected position, which suggested that the recognition motif resides in the 13 C-terminal amino acids of the leader peptide (Figure 4—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF MS data showing cleavage of the synthetic peptide.

claim: The recognition motif for LahT150 resides in the 13 C-terminal amino acids of the leader peptide.
source: This 17-amino acid peptide was cleaved by LahT150 at the expected position, which suggested that the recognition motif resides in the 13 C-terminal amino acids of the leader peptide (Figure 4—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: Inferred from the successful cleavage of a minimal synthetic peptide containing only the last 13 amino acids of the leader peptide.

claim: The precursor peptides for haloduracin β and lacticin 481 were successfully cleaved by LahT150 after GA and GS sequences.
source: The precursor peptides for haloduracin β and lacticin 481, lanthipeptides that have been previously produced in E. coli (Shi et al., 2011; Oman et al., 2012), were also successfully cleaved after GA and GS sequences even though the sequence homology is relatively low (Figure 4D and E; for sequences see Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF MS data showing cleavage products.

claim: Cleavage after the GS sequence was observed for the glycocin precursor peptide SunA.
source: Cleavage after the GS sequence was also observed for the glycocin precursor peptide SunA (Figure 4F) (Oman et al., 2011), demonstrating the extension of the utility of LahT150 to a different RiPP class.
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF MS data showing cleavage of SunA.

claim: Position −3 is almost invariably an Ala in LahT150 substrates.
source: Position −3 is almost invariably an Ala (Figure 4G) but variants of XY33a in which this Ala was mutated to Tyr, Phe, Lys, or Glu were all cleaved by LahT150 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: XY33a variants in which Ala at position −3 was mutated to Tyr, Phe, Lys, or Glu were all cleaved by LahT150.
source: Position −3 is almost invariably an Ala (Figure 4G) but variants of XY33a in which this Ala was mutated to Tyr, Phe, Lys, or Glu were all cleaved by LahT150 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF MS data showing cleavage of mutant peptides.

claim: Mutation of Val at position −4 to Lys or Asp resulted in mutants that were not substrates for LahT150.
source: Mutagenesis to Lys or Asp resulted in mutants that were not substrates for LahT150, but the XY33a V−4T mutant was completely processed.
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF MS data showing no cleavage for V-4K and V-4D mutants.

claim: The XY33a V−4T mutant was completely processed by LahT150.
source: Mutagenesis to Lys or Asp resulted in mutants that were not substrates for LahT150, but the XY33a V−4T mutant was completely processed.
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF MS data showing cleavage of the V-4T mutant.

claim: The nearly invariant Glu at position −5 was not important for LahT150 recognition as mutation to Lys, Ala, and Asp was tolerated.
source: Surprisingly, the nearly invariant Glu at position −5 was not important as mutation to Lys, Ala, and Asp was tolerated (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF MS data showing cleavage of E-5K, E-5A, and E-5D mutants.

claim: Mutation of Glu at position −8 to Lys, Ala, and Asp did not abrogate catalysis by LahT150.
source: The same observation was made for the Glu at position −8, since mutation to Lys, Ala, and Asp did not abrogate catalysis.
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF MS data showing cleavage of E-8K, E-8A, and E-8D mutants.

claim: Mutation of Leu−7 to Lys or Asp had a strong negative effect on catalysis by LahT150.
source: In contrast, mutation of Leu−7 to Lys or Asp had a strong negative effect on catalysis indicating that this residue is important (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF MS data showing no or minimal cleavage for L-7K and L-7D mutants.

claim: Leu−7 is an important residue for LahT150 substrate recognition.
source: In contrast, mutation of Leu−7 to Lys or Asp had a strong negative effect on catalysis indicating that this residue is important (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Inferred from mutagenesis data showing strong negative effects when this residue is mutated.

claim: Mutagenesis of Leu−12 to Ala resulted in a peptide that was partially processed by LahT150.
source: Mutagenesis of Leu−12 to Ala resulted in a peptide that was partially processed by LahT150; however, changing this residue to a Lys, Asp, Phe or Trp significantly impaired cleavage activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF MS data showing partial cleavage of the L-12A mutant.

claim: Changing Leu−12 to Lys, Asp, Phe or Trp significantly impaired LahT150 cleavage activity.
source: Mutagenesis of Leu−12 to Ala resulted in a peptide that was partially processed by LahT150; however, changing this residue to a Lys, Asp, Phe or Trp significantly impaired cleavage activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF MS data showing no or minimal cleavage for L-12K, L-12D, L-12F, and L-12W mutants.

claim: The crystal structure of LahT147 in complex with peptide aldehyde inhibitor 1 was determined at 2.0 Å resolution.
source: Crystallization efforts with the LahT150 expression construct failed, and we reasoned that the presence of flexible regions, including the His6-tag may pose a hindrance. A shorter construct, including residues 1–147 (hereafter LahT147; as identified by secondary structure analysis) and a TEV cleavable His6-tag, was used for crystallography. Incubation of peptide 1 with LahT147 prior to crystallization yielded crystals of the binary complex that diffracted to 2.0 Å resolution.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data collection and refinement statistics.

claim: The overall structure of LahT147 recapitulates the α/β fold observed in other papain-like peptidase C39 members.
source: The overall structure of LahT147 recapitulates the α/β fold observed in the structures of other papain-like peptidase C39 members, wherein a central six-stranded antiparallel β-sheet is surrounded by five α-helices that pack on either side (Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on structural analysis and comparison with known C39 protease structures.

claim: LahT147 contains a central six-stranded antiparallel β-sheet surrounded by five α-helices.
source: The overall structure of LahT147 recapitulates the α/β fold observed in the structures of other papain-like peptidase C39 members, wherein a central six-stranded antiparallel β-sheet is surrounded by five α-helices that pack on either side (Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on the crystal structure of LahT147.

claim: The closest structural homolog of LahT147 is the peptidase domain of the ComA transporter involved in quorum signaling (Ishii et al., 2010) (PDB Code 3K8U; Z-score = 21.1, RMSD of 1.3 Å over 129 aligned Cα atoms).
source: A DALI search against the Protein Data Bank shows that the closest structural homologs include the peptidase domain of the ComA transporter involved in quorum signaling (Ishii et al., 2010) (PDB Code 3K8U; Z-score = 21.1, RMSD of 1.3 Å over 129 aligned Cα atoms), and the protease domain of full-length PCAT1 Lin et al., 2015 (PDB Code 4RY2; Z-score = 18.8, RMSD of 1.8 Å over 128 aligned Cα atoms).
evidence: Based on DALI search results comparing LahT147 structure to known structures in the Protein Data Bank.

claim: Structural similarity is detected between LahT147 and the non-functional C39-like domain (CLD) from the HlyB transporter from the T1SS involved in α-hemolysin secretion (Lecher et al., 2012) (PDB Code 3ZUA; Z-score = 14.5, RMSD of 2.4 Å over 123 aligned Cα atoms).
source: Notably, structural similarity is also detected with the non-functional C39-like domain (CLD) from the HlyB transporter from the T1SS involved in α-hemolysin secretion (Lecher et al., 2012) (PDB Code 3ZUA; Z-score = 14.5, RMSD of 2.4 Å over 123 aligned Cα atoms).
evidence: Based on DALI search results comparing LahT147 structure to known structures in the Protein Data Bank.

claim: The catalytic triad of LahT147 consists of His101, Asp117, and Cys27.
source: The catalytic triad of LahT147 is interspersed among the secondary structural elements, with His101 and Asp117 situated on strands β4 and β5, respectively, and the nucleophilic Cys27 on helix α1, which borders one side of the central sheet assembly.
evidence: Based on structural analysis of the LahT147 crystal structure.

claim: His101 and Asp117 are situated on strands β4 and β5, respectively, in LahT147.
source: The catalytic triad of LahT147 is interspersed among the secondary structural elements, with His101 and Asp117 situated on strands β4 and β5, respectively, and the nucleophilic Cys27 on helix α1, which borders one side of the central sheet assembly.
evidence: Based on structural analysis of the LahT147 crystal structure.

claim: The nucleophilic Cys27 is located on helix α1 in LahT147.
source: The catalytic triad of LahT147 is interspersed among the secondary structural elements, with His101 and Asp117 situated on strands β4 and β5, respectively, and the nucleophilic Cys27 on helix α1, which borders one side of the central sheet assembly.
evidence: Based on structural analysis of the LahT147 crystal structure.

claim: Clear and continuous density corresponding to the peptide aldehyde 1 can be observed bound covalently to Cys27 as a thiohemiacetal in all four crystallographically independent molecules.
source: Clear and continuous density corresponding to the peptide aldehyde 1 can be observed bound covalently to Cys27 as a thiohemiacetal in all four crystallographically independent molecules.
evidence: Based on electron density maps from the crystal structure.

claim: The peptide binds in a groove formed between helices α1–α3 and the central antiparallel β-sheet in LahT147.
source: The peptide binds in a groove formed between helices α1–α3 and the central antiparallel β-sheet (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Based on structural analysis of the LahT147-peptide complex.

claim: The C-terminus of peptide 1 (residues Gly−1 through Ala−3) binds in a linear manner to the corresponding protease subsites.
source: The C-terminus of peptide 1, which consists of residues Gly−1 through Ala−3 that correspond to the P1 through P3 positions of the precursor substrate (per the nomenclature of Schechter and Berger [Schechter and Berger, 1967]) binds in a linear manner to the corresponding protease subsites.
evidence: Based on structural analysis of the LahT147-peptide complex.

claim: Residues Val−4 through Ser−11 of the peptide form a short two-turn helix in the LahT147 complex.
source: In contrast, residues Val−4 through Ser−11 form a short two-turn helix, which positions residues Val−4, Leu−7, and Leu−12 of the leader peptide into a hydrophobic groove in LahT150, located roughly 20 Å away from the active site.
evidence: Based on structural analysis of the LahT147-peptide complex.

claim: Residues Val−4, Leu−7, and Leu−12 of the leader peptide are positioned into a hydrophobic groove in LahT150, located roughly 20 Å away from the active site.
source: In contrast, residues Val−4 through Ser−11 form a short two-turn helix, which positions residues Val−4, Leu−7, and Leu−12 of the leader peptide into a hydrophobic groove in LahT150, located roughly 20 Å away from the active site.
evidence: Based on structural analysis of the LahT147-peptide complex.

claim: Gln21 is located 4.3 Å away from the thiohemiacetal oxygen atom in the LahT147-peptide complex.
source: Prior studies on other AMS protease domains suggested that Gln21 may stabilize the oxyanion upon formation of the tetrahedral intermediate (Ishii et al., 2010), but in the cocrystal structure, this residue is located 4.3 Å away from the thiohemiacetal oxygen atom originating from the former carbonyl group.
evidence: Based on distance measurements in the crystal structure.

claim: The catalytic His101 is positioned in line with the carbonyl oxygen at a distance of 2.7 Å in the LahT147-peptide complex.
source: Another residue that can function in this role is the catalytic His101, which is positioned in line with the carbonyl oxygen at a distance of 2.7 Å.
evidence: Based on distance measurements in the crystal structure.

claim: The catalytic His in proteolytic enzymes can have multiple functional roles.
source: Studies of other proteolytic enzymes, such as the PCY1 macrocyclase involved in orbitide biosynthesis, are also consistent with multiple functional roles for the catalytic His (Chekan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior studies on other proteolytic enzymes.

claim: The surface of LahT147 largely consists of polar residues with the exception of a hydrophobic groove that engages the two-turn helix of the substrate.
source: Mapping the amino acid hydropathy onto a surface rendering of LahT147 (using the Kyte and Doolittle scale [Kyte and Doolittle, 1982] as implemented in the Chimera software package [Pettersen et al., 2004]) reveals that the surface of the protease largely consists of polar residues with the exception of the aforementioned hydrophobic groove that engages the two-turn helix of the substrate (Figure 5D).
evidence: Based on hydropathy analysis of the LahT147 structure.

claim: There is an increase in hydrophobicity in the region flanking the active site of LahT147, which is accompanied by a narrowing of the binding pocket.
source: There is also an increase in hydrophobicity in the region flanking the active site, which is accompanied by a narrowing of the binding pocket.
evidence: Based on hydropathy analysis and structural analysis of LahT147.

claim: The hydrophobic packing interactions between LahT147 and peptide inhibitor 1 provide a rationale for the mutational data showing that LahT147 could not process variants with replacements of Val−4 or Leu−7 with acidic or basic residues.
source: The hydrophobic packing interactions between LahT147 and peptide inhibitor 1 provide a rationale for our mutational data, wherein LahT147 could not process variants of the full-length precursor peptide that contained replacements of either Val−4 or Leu−7 with an acidic or basic residue nor most mutations of Leu−12 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Structural data provides mechanistic explanation for mutagenesis results.

claim: Substrate recognition in LahT147 occurs roughly 20 Å away from the double Gly motif.
source: Our co-crystal structure illustrates that substrate recognition occurs roughly 20 Å away from the double Gly motif, and residues in this region form an α-helix that positions residues Val−4, Leu−7, and Leu−12 of the substrate peptide into a hydrophobic groove in the protease domain.
evidence: Based on structural analysis of the LahT147-peptide complex.

claim: Residues in the substrate recognition region form an α-helix that positions residues Val−4, Leu−7, and Leu−12 of the substrate peptide into a hydrophobic groove in the protease domain.
source: Our co-crystal structure illustrates that substrate recognition occurs roughly 20 Å away from the double Gly motif, and residues in this region form an α-helix that positions residues Val−4, Leu−7, and Leu−12 of the substrate peptide into a hydrophobic groove in the protease domain.
evidence: Based on structural analysis of the LahT147-peptide complex.

claim: The 'knobs-into-holes' type packing in LahT147 is conceptually analogous to leader peptide recognition in RiPP biosynthetic enzymes (Ortega et al., 2015; Koehnke et al., 2015; Grove et al., 2017; Evans et al., 2017).
source: Such 'knobs-into-holes' type packing is conceptually analogous to leader peptide recognition in RiPP biosynthetic enzymes (Ortega et al., 2015; Koehnke et al., 2015; Grove et al., 2017; Evans et al., 2017) wherein hydrophobic residues in the precursor peptide, distal from the core peptide are positioned into suitably arranged nonpolar pockets.
evidence: Comparison to known mechanisms in related enzymes supported by citations.

claim: The structures of LahT147 protease domain and PCAT1 protease domain align with a RMSD of 1.6 Å over 128 Cα atoms despite overall low (~25%) sequence identity.
source: A plausible model for substrate translocation in the context of a full-length AMS/PCAT can be envisioned by superimposing the cocrystal structure of the LahT protease domain onto the structure of full-length PCAT1 in the absence of nucleotides (Lin et al., 2015). Despite overall low (~25%) sequence identity between the respective protease domains, the structures align with a RMSD of 1.6 Å over 128 Cα atoms.
evidence: Based on structural alignment of LahT147 and PCAT1 protease domains.

claim: In the model of full-length AMS/PCAT, the helical region of the substrate peptide is oriented in a small groove located between the protease domain and the nucleotide-binding domain.
source: In the model, the helical region of the substrate peptide is oriented in a small groove located between the protease domain and the nucleotide-binding domain, providing an effective means to lock these domains together.
evidence: Based on modeling studies using the LahT147-peptide structure superimposed on full-length PCAT1.

claim: The substrate peptide cargo would be directed out from the active site of the protease domain and positioned directly into the TMD to facilitate export in the full-length AMS/PCAT model.
source: The substrate peptide cargo would be directed out from the active site of the protease domain and positioned directly into the TMD to facilitate export.
evidence: Based on modeling studies using the LahT147-peptide structure superimposed on full-length PCAT1.

claim: The pocket near the site of proteolysis is increasingly narrow, explaining the identity of small residues at the double Gly cleavage site.
source: This pocket is increasingly narrow near the site of proteolysis, explaining the identity of small residues at the double Gly cleavage site (Figure 6A).
evidence: Structural features provide mechanistic explanation for substrate specificity.

claim: There is an increase in the hydrophobicity of the pocket near the site of proteolysis, which may serve to further direct the substrate into the TMD.
source: There is also an increase in the hydrophobicity of the pocket near this site, which may serve to further direct the substrate into the TMD.
evidence: Based on structural analysis and modeling, with speculative interpretation of function.

claim: The leader peptide may provide a backstop that prevents the cleaved cargo from leaking back into the cytoplasm.
source: The leader peptide may provide a backstop that prevents the cleaved cargo from leaking back into the cytoplasm, and ensuring the extracellular directionality of transport upon binding of ATP to the NBDs.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on structural modeling.

claim: Conformational changes observed in the structure of PCAT1 upon nucleotide binding ensure shuttling of the cleaved cargo to the extracellular region and result in disengagement of the protease domain for subsequent rounds of coupled export.
source: The conformational changes observed in the structure of PCAT1 upon nucleotide binding both ensure shuttling of the cleaved cargo to the extracellular region, and result in disengagement of the protease domain for subsequent rounds of coupled export (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on prior structural studies of PCAT1 cited in the text.

claim: The CLD domain is essential for secretion of hemolysin A (HlyA) mediated by the ABC transporter HlyB, despite lacking proteolytic activity.
source: Analysis of transport of hemolysin A (HlyA) mediated by the ABC transporter HlyB demonstrates that the CLD is essential for secretion, despite lacking proteolytic activity (Lecher et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior studies on HlyB.

claim: Pull-down assays demonstrate that the CLD interacts only with the unfolded HlyA substrate.
source: Pull-down assays demonstrate that the CLD interacts only with the unfolded HlyA substrate, leading to the suggestion that the CLD may play a chaperone-like role.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior studies on HlyB.

claim: The CLD may play a role in stabilizing the nucleotide-free state of HlyB by binding the substrate peptide, which may optimally position the peptide cargo for export upon ATP binding.
source: Our studies suggest that the CLD may also play a role in stabilizing the nucleotide-free state of HlyB by binding the substrate peptide, which may optimally position the peptide cargo for export upon ATP binding.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on structural and biochemical data from this study.

claim: LahT150 is a highly versatile and useful protease for RiPP research as it removes the leader peptide from a remarkably diverse set of peptides including leader peptides of the Nif11 and nitrile hydratase families.
source: This study shows that LahT150 is a highly versatile and useful protease for RiPP research as it removes the leader peptide from a remarkably diverse set of peptides including leader peptides of the Nif11 and nitrile hydratase families.
evidence: Conclusion based on the experimental data showing broad substrate tolerance.

claim: Dual-functional transporters called AMS/PCATs excise a leader sequence concomitant with the unidirectional extracellular export of the mature peptide.
source: The dual-functional transporters, called ABC-transporter maturation and secretion (AMS) proteins or peptidase-containing ATP-binding transporters (PCAT), excise a leader sequence concomitant with the unidirectional extracellular export of the mature peptide (Håvarstein et al., 1995; van Belkum et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In Gram-positive bacteria, the AMS/PCATs export peptides that mediate quorum signaling or exert antimicrobial activity upon removal of the leader peptide.
source: In Gram-positive bacteria, the AMS/PCATs export peptides that mediate quorum signaling (Pestova et al., 1996) or exert antimicrobial activity upon removal of the leader peptide (van Belkum et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Peptide substrates for AMS/PCAT transporters contain leader sequences that typically end in a double Gly motif (Gly-Gly; Gly-Ala; Gly-Ser).
source: Peptide substrates for the transporters contain leader sequences that typically end in a double Gly motif (Gly-Gly; Gly-Ala; Gly-Ser), and mutational analysis of the ComA transporter identified a consensus recognition sequence of Leu(−12)-(X)3-Glu(−8)-Leu(−7) located N-terminal to this double Gly motif (Ishii et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior studies.

claim: Mutational analysis of the ComA transporter identified a consensus recognition sequence of Leu(−12)-(X)3-Glu(−8)-Leu(−7) located N-terminal to the double Gly motif.
source: Peptide substrates for the transporters contain leader sequences that typically end in a double Gly motif (Gly-Gly; Gly-Ala; Gly-Ser), and mutational analysis of the ComA transporter identified a consensus recognition sequence of Leu(−12)-(X)3-Glu(−8)-Leu(−7) located N-terminal to this double Gly motif (Ishii et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior studies.

claim: In Gram-negative bacteria, the AMS/PCATs are a component of a membrane protein complex containing an outer membrane protein/factor (OMF) and an accessory protein to form the type I secretion system (T1SS).
source: In Gram-negative bacteria, the AMS/PCATs are a component of a membrane protein complex containing an outer membrane protein/factor (OMF) and an accessory protein to form the type I secretion system (T1SS) (Létoffé et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior studies.

claim: Some T1SS complexes contain an AMS/PCAT transporter that lacks proteolytic activity due to the absence of the catalytically requisite Cys, and their N-terminal extension has been named C39-like domain (CLD).
source: Some T1SS complexes contain an AMS/PCAT transporter that lacks proteolytic activity due to the absence of the catalytically requisite Cys, and their N-terminal extension has thus been named C39-like domain (CLD) (Kanonenberg et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior studies.

claim: The CLD domain is necessary to recruit and tether the unfolded substrate during secretion through a yet-to-be established mechanism.
source: Despite the lack of proteolytic activity, the CLD domain is necessary to recruit and tether the unfolded substrate during secretion through a yet-to-be established mechanism (Lecher et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior studies.

claim: The structure of full-length PCAT1 demonstrated that the protease domain interacts with a transmembrane channel in the absence of bound nucleotide.
source: The structure of a full-length PCAT from Clostridium thermocellum (termed PCAT1), containing both the C39 protease and the ABC transporter, demonstrated that the protease domain interacts with a transmembrane channel in the absence of bound nucleotide (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior structural studies.

claim: Binding of ATP results in the disengagement of the protease domain from the helices of the transmembrane domain (TMD) in PCAT1, suggesting an 'alternating-access' model for peptide translocation.
source: Binding of ATP results in the disengagement of the protease domain from the helices of the transmembrane domain (TMD), suggesting an 'alternating-access' model for peptide translocation.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior structural studies.

claim: Biochemical studies of PCAT1 using a peptide substrate showed that proteolytic activity is enhanced during association with the TMD.
source: Notably, biochemical studies of PCAT1 using a peptide substrate showed that proteolytic activity is enhanced during association with the TMD, but the underpinnings of this enhancement were unclear in the absence of a peptide substrate-bound structure.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior biochemical studies.

claim: Association with the TMD significantly enhances proteolytic activity of the protease domain in PCAT1 and NukT.
source: The lack of activity for these excised C39 protein domains is not unexpected, given prior studies that show that association with the TMD significantly enhances proteolytic activity of the protease domain in PCAT1 (Lin et al., 2015) and NukT (Nishie et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The lah gene cluster in Lachnospiraceae bacterium C6A11 encodes nine different putative precursor peptides (LahA1-9) with diverse core peptide sequences and relatively conserved double Gly-motif leader peptides of the Nif11 type.
source: We next investigated an AMS/PCAT transporter LahT encoded in a gene cluster in a member of the human commensal microbiota, Lachnospiraceae bacterium C6A11 (genome from Bioproject ID 223496/Accession PRJNA223496). This cluster encodes nine different putative precursor peptides (LahA1-9) with diverse core peptide sequences and relatively conserved double Gly-motif leader peptides of the Nif11 type (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on genomic analysis and sequence alignment.

claim: Prochlorococcus MIT9313 encodes 30 different RiPP substrates with leader peptides of the double Gly type.
source: We initially focused on the N-terminal protease domain of a transporter in Prochlorococcus MIT9313, which encodes 30 different RiPP substrates with leader peptides of the double Gly type (Li et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior studies.

claim: The FlvT transporter from Ruminococcus flavefaciens FD-1 is encoded in a cluster with 12 substrate peptides.
source: We next turned to the protease domain of the FlvT transporter from Ruminococcus flavefaciens FD-1, encoded in a cluster with 12 substrate peptides (Zhao and van der Donk, 2016), but it also did not provide the desired robust activity.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior studies.

claim: Lachnospiraceae bacterium C6A11 is a member of the human commensal microbiota.
source: We next investigated an AMS/PCAT transporter LahT encoded in a gene cluster in a member of the human commensal microbiota, Lachnospiraceae bacterium C6A11 (genome from Bioproject ID 223496/Accession PRJNA223496).
evidence: Based on knowledge of the organism's ecological niche.

claim: The N-terminal 150 amino acids of AMS/PCAT proteins constitute peptidase C39 family members that can be expressed as individual active domains.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that the N-terminal 150 amino acids of AMS/PCAT proteins constitute peptidase C39 family members that can be expressed as individual active domains (Håvarstein et al., 1995; Furgerson Ihnken et al., 2008; Ishii et al., 2006; Wu and Tai, 2004; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Crystallographic phases for the LahT147-peptide complex were determined by the single wavelength anomalous diffraction method using data from a mercury-soaked crystal.
source: Crystallographic phases were determined by the single wavelength anomalous diffraction method via AutoSol (Terwilliger et al., 2009) from data collected on a crystal soaked in precipitant solution with additional 2 mM 4-chloromercuribenzenesulfonate (PCMBS) for 2 hr.
evidence: Based on crystallographic methods described in the text.

claim: The crystallographic asymmetric unit of the LahT147-peptide complex contains four copies of the complex.
source: The crystallographic asymmetric unit contains four copies of the complex allowing for multiple independent and unbiased views of the protein-peptide complex structure.
evidence: Based on crystallographic data.

claim: Peptide aldehyde inhibitors have been used successfully to obtain covalently bound inhibitors of Cys proteases.
source: LahT150 is a Cys protease, and substrate analogs terminating in an aldehyde at the scissile amide have been used successfully to obtain covalently bound inhibitors (Westerik and Wolfenden, 1972; Thompson, 1973).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Peptide 1 represents the C-terminal 13 amino acids of the ProcA2.8 leader peptide with an aldehyde in the terminal position.
source: We therefore synthesized peptide 1 representing the C-terminal 13 amino acids of the ProcA2.8 leader peptide with an aldehyde in the terminal position (Figure 4H).
evidence: Based on the design and synthesis of the inhibitor described in the text.

claim: RiPPs are made from a precursor peptide that is morphed into a final bioactive product with a much larger structural diversity than can be achieved with the 20 proteinogenic amino acids.
source: RiPPs are made from a precursor peptide that is morphed into a final bioactive product with a much larger structural diversity than can be achieved with the 20 proteinogenic amino acids.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about RiPP biosynthesis.

claim: During RiPP biosynthesis, posttranslational modification enzymes often act iteratively on a subset of amino acids present in a C-terminal core peptide in a process that is directed by an N-terminal leader peptide.
source: During this process, posttranslational modification enzymes often act iteratively on a subset of amino acids present in a C-terminal core peptide in a process that is directed by an N-terminal leader peptide (Oman and van der Donk, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior studies.

claim: Following the installation of posttranslational modifications, the cognate AMS/PCAT catalyzes the removal of the leader peptide via cleavage at the double Gly motif and extracellular secretion of the bioactive natural product.
source: Following the installation of these posttranslational modifications, the cognate AMS/PCAT catalyzes the removal of the leader peptide via cleavage at the double Gly motif and extracellular secretion of the bioactive natural product (Håvarstein et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior studies.

claim: Two particularly large classes of double-Gly leader peptides belong to the Nif11 and nitrile hydratase families.
source: Two particularly large classes of these double-Gly leader peptides belong to the Nif11 and nitrile hydratase families (Haft et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior studies.

claim: The dual-functional transporters must ensure that modified and processed bacteriocins or RiPPs are directly shuttled out of the producing organism.
source: Notably, the dual-functional transporters must ensure that modified and processed bacteriocins or RiPPs are directly shuttled out of the producing organism but the details for this fail-safe mechanism are not yet known.
evidence: Statement of an unsolved problem in the field.

claim: The details for the fail-safe mechanism ensuring direct shuttling of processed RiPPs out of the producing organism are not yet known.
source: Notably, the dual-functional transporters must ensure that modified and processed bacteriocins or RiPPs are directly shuttled out of the producing organism but the details for this fail-safe mechanism are not yet known.
evidence: Statement of an unsolved problem in the field.

claim: Developing general methods for leader peptide removal has been challenging, especially for the double Gly leader peptides.
source: However, developing general methods for leader peptide removal has been challenging (Li et al., 2010; Shi et al., 2011; Goto et al., 2010; Plat et al., 2011; Lohans et al., 2014; Ökesli et al., 2011), especially for the double Gly leader peptides.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: RiPPs are attractive for genome mining and synthetic biology because of the direct link between the genome-encoded precursor peptide and the final natural product.
source: Because of the direct link between the genome-encoded precursor peptide and the final natural product, RiPPs are attractive for genome mining (Velásquez and van der Donk, 2011; Hetrick and van der Donk, 2017) and synthetic biology (Yang et al., 2018; Sardar et al., 2015; Burkhart et al., 2017; van Heel et al., 2013; Montalbán-López et al., 2017; Urban et al., 2017; Hetrick et al., 2018), and numerous studies have described the successful reconstitution of RiPP machinery in heterologous hosts, including E. coli.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: In many genome mining exercises, the leader peptide is not removed inside the heterologous host to prevent potential toxicity of the final compound.
source: In many such genome mining exercises, the leader peptide is not removed inside the heterologous host to prevent potential toxicity of the final compound (Valsesia et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior studies.

claim: Retaining the leader peptide during heterologous production enables attachment of an affinity tag that allows one-step purification.
source: An additional advantage of retaining the leader peptide during heterologous production is that it enables attachment of an affinity tag that allows one-step purification, which avoids tedious purification of compounds that may be produced in small quantities (Shi et al., 2011; Nagao et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.
